items.description: The Nerd opens in a lab, on an operating table, then plays a Super NES cart and an NES one with a password screen. A story about a creature stitched together should expect some seams.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/CD-I (Part 1) Hotel Mario - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 59.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: CD-i (Part 1): Hotel Mario
items.description: A tour of the Nerd's Philips shelf leads to a game where the plumber's whole job is closing doors in a hotel. First of three. The doors do close, and nobody promised more.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/CD-I (Part 2) Zelda Wand of Gamelon - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 60.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: CD-i (Part 2): Zelda: Wand of Gamelon
items.description: Part two puts the princess in the lead, among painted backdrops and cartoon cutscenes. The Nerd measures it against the Hyrule he knows. It is certainly a change of pace.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/CD-I (Part 3) Faces of Evil  Zelda's Adventure - Angry Video Game - Episode 61.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: CD-i (Part 3)
items.description: The CD-i finale: Link: The Faces of Evil, then Zelda's Adventure, with the princess back in the lead on an overhead map. The Nerd reaches the end of the shelf, and the shelf has a lot to answer for.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Bible Games 2 - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 62.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Bible Games 2
items.description: Round two of the Nerd's faith-based games ends on a disc menu offering a sing-along with Moses and the Pharaoh. A sing-along is a feature the material was built for.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Michael Jackson's Moonwalker - Sega Genesis - Angry Video Game Nerd Episode 63.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Michael Jackson's Moonwalker
items.description: Gangsters, kidnapped kids and a dance move that clears the room, all on the Genesis, with a robot suit near the end. Every problem here has the same solution, and the game knows it.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Milon's Secret Castle - NES - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 64.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Milon's Secret Castle
items.description: A Hudson Soft NES castle where the way forward is usually a wall nobody told you to try. A shop sells hints, which is considerate of it, since the walls offer none.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Atari Jaguar (Part 1) - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 65.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Atari Jaguar (Part 1)
items.description: A lap of other consoles' controllers leads to Atari's self-billed 64-bit machine, whose own pad carries a full numeric keypad. Ready to dial, as it were. The Nerd reviews the hardware first.

items.title: X-Play: Silent Hill Downpour, UFC Undisputed 3
items.description: Silent Hill: Downpour, whose title doubles as the forecast, gets a gameplay preview. UFC Undisputed 3 gets an exclusive, and Irrational Games' art director walks through BioShock Infinite.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Atari Jaguar (Part 2) - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 66.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Atari Jaguar (Part 2)
items.description: Doom turns up for the second half, then a kilted brawler whose options menu has a setting called Gore Fest. Few menus have ever described their contents so accurately.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Metal Gear - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 67.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Metal Gear
items.description: Snake's NES mission runs through jungle, past supply trucks and into a fortress, and the equipment menu lists cigarettes. A careful soldier travels with a full kit.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Odyssey - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 68.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Odyssey
items.description: A white dot on a blue screen, two dials to steer it, and a plastic overlay clinging to the glass for scenery. Scorekeeping is left to the player, which is a fair deal for a dot.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/X-Men - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 69.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: X-Men
items.description: Wolverine's cartridge opens on a future where mutantkind is gone and Sentinels have the run of the place. Each hero comes with a strength meter, the one number the game wants you watching.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Terminator - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 70.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Terminator
items.description: The NES game opens the tour: a soldier in green fatigues crosses ruined rooftops, ledges and girders. The future war is mostly a platforming problem, and the level designer found a lot of ledges.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Terminator (Part 2) - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 71.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Terminator (Part 2)
items.description: Judgment Day gets a tour of the Super NES, Game Boy and arcade versions, each one walking into the same bar and onto the same motorcycle. The film left two set pieces, and every version used both.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Transformers - Famicom - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 72.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Transformers
items.description: Imports are the plan: a Famicom cartridge, Japanese packaging, and a hero who is a robot on one screen and a jet on the next. Transforming was the one thing the toy promised, and the game delivers it.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Mario is Missing - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 73.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Mario Is Missing
items.description: Luigi searches real cities for Mario, with trivia stops like a fill-in-the-blank about Jefferson in Philadelphia. Edutainment promised a lesson with a plumber attached, and this one does show its work.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Plumbers Don't Wear Ties - Panasonic 3DO - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 74.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Plumbers Don't Wear Ties
items.description: The Nerd plays a 3DO game built from live-action romance clips, on a Panasonic REAL. The game captions its own plot, "He makes a first move," in case the footage left any doubt. Thoughtful of it.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Bugs Bunny's Crazy Castle - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 75.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Bugs Bunny's Crazy Castle
items.description: Bugs climbs castle stairs for carrots, and every stage ends with a password to write down. Meanwhile a full-size rabbit costume turns up in the Nerd's basement, and Woody Woodpecker gets a castle of his own.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Super Pitfall - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 76.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Super Pitfall
items.description: Pitfall Harry returns on the NES, working down caves of ladders and ledges where progress depends on items nobody can see. Exploration in the full sense: you find out by falling.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Godzilla - NES, SNES - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 77.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Godzilla
items.description: The King of the Monsters walks across the NES, a hex-board strategy map and a 3D brawler, and a yellow arrow points out his mechanical double's life bar. Size, in these games, is mostly travel time.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Wayne's World - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 78.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Wayne's World
items.description: A movie about a basement cable show becomes a platformer twice, NES first and Super NES second, with the car singalong cut in. The basement, as a stage, is a bold place to start scrolling.

items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Castlevania
items.description: Candles lit, the Nerd takes on the NES vampire hunt that began Konami's long run of castles, stopping at the manual's item chart. The castle's rules are posted, which is more than most castles manage.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Castlevania (Part 2) - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 80.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Castlevania (Part 2)
items.description: A sequel sends Simon Belmont from town to town, and the Nerd holds the manual's crystal page up to the camera as evidence. The case against this game has a lot of exhibits.

items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Castlevania (Part 3)
items.description: Simon Belmont swings his whip on the Super NES, then Carrie walks into three dimensions on the Nintendo 64. The candles come along, and now they have depth.

items.title: Cinematech: Gala-ga ga
items.description: Phantasy Star Online's intro sends Pioneer 1 to find a habitable planet, and the episode closes on rows of aliens above a lone cannon. Colony ship first, then a gun at the bottom. The order is correct.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Castlevania (Part 4) - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 82.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Castlevania (Part 4)
items.description: Genesis, PlayStation, Nintendo 64: the Nerd follows the vampire series across three consoles. Dracula asks what a man is, which is a lot to put to a player who only wants a save point.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Little Red Hood - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 83.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Little Red Hood
items.description: A fairy-tale girl crosses an NES forest made mostly of palm trees, and the Nerd follows her through every screen. The route is long, and the scenery is committed to staying the same.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Winter Games - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 84.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Winter Games
items.description: The Nerd bundles up for a winter sports cartridge, and the scoreboard answers with 0.0 after 0.0 while a computer pacer skates beside him. The scoring is honest about what it was given.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Street Fighter 2010 - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 85.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Street Fighter 2010
items.description: The intro crawl puts Ken in space after his partner Troy is lost, and the Nerd keeps asking where the fighting went. The one link to the arcade is a name, and the cartridge guards it carefully.

items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Hydlide
items.description: An old Japanese computer RPG reaches the NES by way of FCI, and the Nerd tours its fields of kobolds, where fighting means walking into things. The method never varies.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Ninja Gaiden - Angry Video Game Nerd.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Ninja Gaiden
items.description: Ryu Hayabusa crosses Tecmo's NES stages, each followed by a cinema scene, while a ninja drops in on the Nerd mid-review. The game's advice is to keep moving, and it is hard to argue.

items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: SwordQuest
items.description: Atari hid the clues in comic books packed with the cartridges and put a prize on the solution. Fireworld and Waterworld get a play. A quest that needs a second medium is still a quest.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Pong Consoles - Angry Video Game Nerd.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Pong Consoles
items.description: Wonder Wizard and its cousins line up for the Nerd: a ball, two paddles, a knob or a slider. Each console is the whole game, and the design got it right the first time.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Action 52 - Angry Video Game Nerd - Cinemassacre.com.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Action 52
items.description: One NES cartridge lists fifty-two games, and the Nerd scrolls the menu to the last entry to confirm it. The pitch was quantity, and on the menu screen the pitch holds.

items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Cheetahmen
items.description: Action 52 bet its fifty-two-game cartridge on one franchise, and the Nerd plays down the menu to find it. Three cat heroes were meant to carry a whole brand, and he checks how far they got.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Game Glitches - Angry Video Game Nerd.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Game Glitches
items.description: The Nerd collects the screens that go wrong across the NES and beyond, and a green gremlin takes the blame. As explanations go, it beats a dirty cartridge.

items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Zelda 2
items.description: Zelda II sends Link sideways, with experience levels, towns and a villager named Error. The game keeps a straight face about all three.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Back to the Future ReRevisited - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 94.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Back to the Future ReRevisited
items.description: The Nerd returns to Back to the Future on the NES, with Hill Valley's map, the LJN logo and a Western Part III in tow. A time-travel game earns a second visit on principle.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde Revisited - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 95.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde Revisited
items.description: The Nerd, caped, returns to Bandai's NES Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, beaker in hand. The premise is the title: one man, two sides, and a town that objects to both.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Lester the Unlikely - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 96.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Lester the Unlikely
items.description: A Super NES platformer maroons its hero on a jungle island with a turtle for a bridge, and the Nerd crosses, falls and crosses again. The turtle is the most dependable thing in the game.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/How the Nerd Stole Christmas - Angry Video Game Nerd - Episode 97.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: How the Nerd Stole Christmas
items.description: The Nerd plays Grinch in a Seuss-style illustrated Christmas special, creeping to a tree stacked with cartridges. Games under the tree is the right instinct, and the tape treats it that way.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Day Dreamin Davey - Angry Video Game Nerd.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Day Dreamin' Davey
items.description: Davey daydreams his way into a Western town and a Greek temple, and the Nerd follows him through. As dream logic goes, the game is thorough: nothing is explained.

items.id: AVGNCompleteCollection/Star Wars Games - Angry Video Game Nerd.ia.mp4
items.title: The Angry Video Game Nerd: Star Wars Games
items.description: A snowspeeder run on the Atari, Tatooine on the NES, Luke on the Super NES: the Nerd takes the saga one console at a time. In most of these the Force is a jump button, and they commit to it.

items.title: Good Eating Habits
items.description: One boy's stomachache gets a full investigation: gulped breakfast, bolted lunch, soda, and a food nightmare as the verdict. The advice is to chew. It is hard to argue.

items.title: How to Be Well Groomed
items.description: Clean fingernails, pressed shirts, and a fresh haircut. This film believes good grooming isn't vanity — it's respect for yourself and everyone around you. Don could use this advice.

items.title: Dating: Do's and Don'ts
items.description: Woody's taking a girl to the Hi-Teen Carnival for the first time. Should he hold the door? Pay for popcorn? This one covers it all with helpful diagrams of what constitutes acceptable behavior.

items.title: Date With Your Family, A
items.description: A family sits down to dinner together. Father carves the roast. Mother serves. Everyone uses their napkin. This Simmel-Meservey classic demonstrates the idealized American family dinner — every fork in its place.

items.title: Social-Sex Attitudes in Adolescence
items.description: A frank discussion of the facts of life for teenagers, handled with the clinical detachment of a science textbook and the awkwardness of a parent who read the manual five minutes ago.

items.title: Good Table Manners
items.description: Elbows off the table. Chew with your mouth closed. Wait for everyone to be served. The fundamentals of table manners presented with the gravity of a military briefing.

items.title: How Much Affection?
items.description: How far is too far? This guidance film tackles the question every 1950s teenager was asking and every 1950s parent was dreading. The answer involves respect, timing, and several uncomfortable pauses.

items.title: This Charming Couple
items.description: A courtship between two people in love with somebody they made up. It starts in divorce court, so you know the ending, and the poetry has a lot to answer for.

items.title: Cindy Goes to a Party
items.description: A tomboy gets a fairy godmother whose whole job is to fix the tomboy part. The rules arrive in superimposed type: Don't break things. Leave on time. Directed by Herk Harvey of Carnival of Souls.

items.title: Are You Ready for Marriage?
items.description: Sue and Larry think they're ready to get married right out of high school. The marriage counselor has some questions for them. Pointed ones.

items.title: Act Your Age
items.description: Are you the one who still throws tantrums? Makes excuses? Blames others? This film has a chart showing what age-appropriate behavior looks like. You might not like where you land.

items.title: Shy Guy
items.description: Phil is smart and kind but he can't talk to people. He freezes up in social situations. This Coronet classic follows his journey from wallflower to functioning member of society.

items.title: Habit Patterns
items.description: You bite your nails. You slouch. You leave your homework to the last minute. This film explains that your habits define your character — and it has the visual aids to prove it.

items.title: What to Do on a Date
items.description: Nick is taking Kay out. Should they go to the movies? A dance? A community event? This step-by-step guide to date planning treats teenage socializing like a logistical operation.

items.title: Everyday Courtesy
items.description: Hold the door. Say please and thank you. Don't interrupt. The basics of civilized behavior, presented as though the future of democracy depends on them. Which, according to this film, it does.

items.title: Maintaining Classroom Discipline
items.description: A practical guide for teachers on keeping order without raising your voice. The methods haven't changed much in seventy years. The haircuts have.

items.title: What Makes A Good Party?
items.description: Games? Music? Refreshments? The art of throwing a party that people actually enjoy, broken down into steps so simple that even your most awkward friend could follow them.

items.title: Beginning to Date
items.description: You're old enough to date but you've never done it. Where do you start? This film walks you through the terrifying first steps of asking someone out, speaking to them, and surviving the experience.

items.title: Going Steady?
items.description: Jeff and Marie are going steady. Is that a good idea? Their parents have concerns. The guidance counselor has a chart. This film has opinions about all of it.

items.title: How Do You Know It's Love?
items.description: Is it love or is it infatuation? This film provides a checklist to help you tell the difference. Spoiler: if you're a teenager, the film is pretty sure it's infatuation.

items.title: The Prom: It's A Pleasure!
items.description: The prom is coming and everything must be perfect — the decorations, the band, the corsage, and most importantly, your behavior. A guide to surviving the biggest night of your young life.

items.title: Control Your Emotions
items.description: You're angry. You're jealous. You're afraid. This Coronet film says: that's normal. Now here's how to stop letting your emotions run the show. Deep breaths. Rational thinking. A firm handshake.

items.title: Office Etiquette
items.description: The telephone is ringing. A visitor has arrived. Your desk is a mess. This guide to office behavior covers everything from proper phone etiquette to not gossiping at the water cooler.

items.title: Choosing for Happiness
items.description: How do you choose a spouse? A career? A way of life? This film believes happiness is a series of informed decisions, and it's here to help you make them correctly.

items.title: I Want to Be a Secretary
items.description: A young woman's journey into the secretarial profession. Filing, typing, shorthand, and the satisfaction of a well-organized desk drawer. The career dream of 1941.

items.title: Family Life
items.description: What does a healthy family look like? This film examines family dynamics with the earnest belief that showing people a model household will fix everything wrong with their own.

items.title: Who's Boss?
items.description: Who makes the decisions in your house? Father? Mother? A family conference? This early film tackles household authority with a directness that hasn't aged gracefully.

items.title: New Girl in the Office (Part II)
items.description: The new hire starts work, and the welcome is stiff enough to file. One employee would rather not work at all than work under the new policy. Integration, by committee.

items.title: The Bully
items.description: There's a bully in school and everyone knows who he is. This film shows how a community can address aggressive behavior — with compassion, firmness, and a visit to the principal's office.

items.title: How to Say No: Moral Maturity
items.description: Peer pressure is real and this film knows it. How do you say no to your friends without losing them? The answer involves backbone, conviction, and a very calm speaking voice.

items.title: Junior Prom
items.description: A 1946 guide to proper dating behavior at the junior prom. What to wear, what to say, and how to be a gentleman on the most important social occasion of the school year.

items.title: Cheating
items.description: You looked at someone else's paper during the test. Was it cheating? This Centron film explores academic honesty through a scenario that will make every student squirm.

items.title: Don't Be Afraid
items.description: A child's fears — of the dark, of dogs, of thunderstorms — examined with patience and practical advice. Being afraid doesn't make you weak. Running from your fears does.

items.title: As Others See Us
items.description: Webster Groves High students demonstrate manners for a narrator who talks down to them the entire time. The goal is sparing you embarrassment. The Dairy Council of St. Louis footed the bill.

items.title: Mental Health: Keeping Mentally Fit
items.description: Your mind needs exercise just like your body. This film prescribes four steps: express your emotions, respect yourself, respect others, solve problems as they arise. The 1952 approach to therapy.

items.title: School Rules: How They Help Us
items.description: Why do we have rules? This educational film makes the case that school rules aren't restrictions — they're the foundation of a functioning society. Start small. Think big.

items.title: Dinner Party
items.description: Soup, meat, dessert, and a large helping of guilt. A teenage birthday dinner becomes a full inspection, and every wrong move is noted. Please enjoy your meal, if you dare.

items.title: Better Use of Leisure Time
items.description: You have free time. Are you wasting it? This film believes that leisure should be productive, enriching, and preferably involve a library card or a community sports league.

items.title: Gossip
items.description: Someone told someone who told someone else, and now the whole school knows something that isn't true. The anatomy of gossip, traced from whisper to catastrophe.

items.title: How Quiet Helps at School
items.description: The classroom is for learning. Not for whispering, not for fidgeting, not for passing notes. A gentle but firm reminder that silence is the sound of education happening.

items.title: What About Juvenile Delinquency?
items.description: Teens in trouble, broken homes, bad influences — this 1955 film examines the roots of juvenile delinquency and suggests that community involvement is the cure. Herk Harvey directs.

items.title: The Snob
items.description: Sarah thinks she's better than everyone else. She's not invited to parties anymore. This Centron film uses social exile to teach the dangers of thinking too highly of yourself.

items.title: Date With Your Family, A (outtakes)
items.description: The outtakes from "A Date With Your Family" — the moments that didn't make it into the polished final cut. The family is less perfect than they seemed. Reality peeks through.

items.title: Age of Turmoil
items.description: Adolescence is turbulent. Your body is changing, your emotions are unpredictable, and your parents don't understand you. This film says: that's completely normal. Now sit down and listen.

items.title: The Benefits of Looking Ahead
items.description: Do you plan ahead or do you live for today? This film makes a compelling case for thinking about tomorrow, complete with cautionary examples of people who didn't.

items.title: Toward Emotional Maturity
items.description: Growing up means learning to handle disappointment, frustration, and not getting your way. This film provides a roadmap from childish reactions to mature responses.

items.title: Mind Your Manners
items.description: Please and thank you. Don't talk back. Respect your elders. The fundamentals of polite behavior, presented to young Americans as the building blocks of civilized life.

items.title: Johnny Learns His Manners
items.description: A boy is turned into a pig for his slovenly manners, which he keeps up so no one calls him a sissy. His mother's rebuttal is a film of West Point cadets. Cartoon logic, military backing.

items.title: Let's Be Good Citizens at School
items.description: What does it mean to be a good citizen at school? This film has specific examples involving hallway behavior, cafeteria conduct, and the proper care of school property.

items.title: Self-Conscious Guy
items.description: He's aware of every flaw, real or imagined. He avoids photographs, dances, and public speaking. This film gently suggests that self-consciousness is a habit, not a life sentence.

items.title: Is This Love?
items.description: Is what you're feeling real love or just a crush? A guidance film that attempts to quantify the most unquantifiable human emotion using checklists and narrator commentary.

items.title: Ways to Settle Disputes
items.description: Two kids want the same toy. Two countries want the same border. This film suggests that the same principles of compromise apply to both. Start in the sandbox, end with world peace.

items.title: The Fun of Being Thoughtful
items.description: Being thoughtful isn't hard — it just requires paying attention to the people around you. This film makes kindness look like the most practical skill you can develop.

items.title: Dining Together
items.description: A family meal is more than food — it's a lesson in cooperation, conversation, and the proper deployment of silverware. Everything has a place. Everyone has a role.

items.title: Your Family
items.description: Your family is the most important group you'll ever belong to. This film examines what makes families work — shared responsibilities, mutual respect, and a father who reads the newspaper quietly.

items.title: Am I Trustworthy?
items.description: Can your friends count on you? Does your word mean something? This film uses a series of everyday scenarios to test whether you're the kind of person people can trust.

items.title: Understand Your Emotions
items.description: You're upset. Do you know why? This Coronet film argues that understanding your emotions is the first step to controlling them, and controlling them is the first step to being an adult.

items.title: How to Keep a Job
items.description: You got the job. Now how do you keep it? Punctuality, attitude, reliability, and knowing when to ask questions versus when to figure things out yourself.

items.title: Helping Johnny Remember
items.description: Nobody will play with this boy, and his former friends are happy to say why: selfish, bossy, hogs the blue paint. The film's fix is a mirror and a choice between Smiley and Sulky.

items.title: Holiday From Rules
items.description: What would happen if there were no rules for one day? This film conducts the thought experiment and reaches a very clear conclusion: rules exist for excellent reasons.

items.title: Law and Social Controls
items.description: Why do we have laws? Where do they come from? Who decides what's fair? A primer on civic responsibility that starts with traffic signals and ends with the Constitution.

items.title: Beginning Responsibility: Taking Care of Things
items.description: Taking care of your toys, your books, and your bicycle isn't just about stuff — it's about building character. This film for younger students teaches responsibility one broken crayon at a time.

items.title: Social Courtesy
items.description: The art of being polite in everyday situations — introducing yourself, making small talk, and navigating the minefield of social interaction with grace and a firm handshake.

items.title: Understanding Your Ideals
items.description: What do you stand for? What matters to you? This film asks teenagers to examine their values and figure out if they're living up to them. The narrator already suspects you're not.

items.title: Office Courtesy: Meeting the Public
items.description: You represent your company every time you answer the phone or greet a visitor. This training film teaches front-desk workers to be friendly, efficient, and unfailingly professional.

items.title: Developing Self-Reliance
items.description: Stop asking for help with things you can do yourself. This film's message is blunt: independence is a muscle, and the only way to build it is to stop relying on everyone else.

items.title: How Do You Do?
items.description: The fundamentals of meeting people — eye contact, a firm handshake, and remembering names. Basic social skills presented as the keys to professional and personal success.

items.title: Overcoming Fear
items.description: Everyone is afraid of something. This film normalizes fear and then systematically explains how to face it. The advice is practical: start small, be brave, repeat.

items.title: Snap Out of It! (Emotional Balance)
items.description: Having a bad day? Feeling sorry for yourself? This film's prescription: snap out of it. Balance your emotions, focus on what you can control, and stop making everything about you.

items.title: How Honest Are You?
items.description: A moral inventory disguised as a classroom film. Would you return a wallet full of cash? Would you tell the truth if lying was easier? This film is watching your face for the answer.

items.title: Attitudes and Health
items.description: Your attitude affects your health — and this 1949 film has the charts to prove it. Positive thinking, regular exercise, and a can-do spirit are presented as literal medicine.

items.title: The Outsider
items.description: Susan Jane doesn't fit in. The class doesn't know what to make of someone different. A guidance film about inclusion that's more relevant now than when it was made.

items.title: Who's Right?
items.description: Two sides of an argument, both convinced they're right. This film presents both cases and asks: how do you decide who's right when everyone believes they are?

items.title: Friendship Begins At Home
items.description: Friendship starts at home — with your siblings, your parents, and the family dog. If you can get along with the people you live with, the rest of the world is easy.

items.title: Table Manners
items.description: Napkin in your lap. Elbows off the table. Don't start eating until everyone is served. The rules of table manners, presented with the seriousness of a military code of conduct.

items.title: Emotional Maturity
items.description: The difference between a mature person and an immature one isn't age — it's how they handle frustration, disappointment, and not getting the last slice of cake.

items.title: New Girl in the Office (Part I)
items.description: The government's contracts committee made this to talk offices into hiring Black employees. Ed Asner is in it, young. It is as stiff and earnest as a memo, and the office is the one squirming.

items.title: Marriage Today
items.description: Marriage in 1950: shared budgets, divided chores, and the art of compromise. This film presents partnership as a practical arrangement that works best when both people try.

items.title: The Trouble Maker
items.description: He disrupts class, picks fights, and doesn't follow rules. But why? This Herk Harvey film looks past the behavior to find the person underneath the trouble.

items.title: Censorship: A Question of Judgment?
items.description: Should the school paper print a photo of a fight, and who gets to decide, the students or the teacher who sponsors it? Freedom of the press, with a hall pass.

items.title: Measure of a Man
items.description: What makes a man? Not muscles or bravado — character, integrity, and the willingness to do the right thing when no one is watching. At least, that's what this film believes.

items.title: The Gossip
items.description: She told one person. That person told two more. By lunch, the whole school had heard a version of the truth that wasn't true at all. The destructive path of a rumor, traced to its source.

items.title: Your Thrift Habits
items.description: A piggy bank, a savings account, and the discipline to not buy everything you want. This 1948 film on thrift treats money management as a moral virtue.

items.title: Writing Better Social Letters
items.description: Thank-you notes, invitations, and letters of apology. The lost art of written social correspondence, taught with penmanship standards that would make a calligrapher weep.

items.title: You and Your Family
items.description: Your role in the family — as a child, a sibling, a member of a team. This film argues that the family unit is practice for citizenship, and your chores are patriotic duty.

items.title: Let's Play Fair
items.description: Taking turns, sharing toys, and not crying when you lose. The earliest lessons in social behavior, presented for the elementary school set with gentle narration and clear examples.

items.title: The Other Fellow
items.description: Chevrolet wants you to drive politely, so it hired Edgar Kennedy to say so. A reckless driver sees himself behind every other wheel on the road. It is safety by comedy, sold by a car company.

items.title: The Procrastinator
items.description: You'll do it tomorrow. You'll start next week. You'll get to it eventually. This Herk Harvey film diagnoses procrastination as a character flaw and prescribes immediate action.

items.title: Playing Together
items.description: Children playing together — sharing, cooperating, taking turns. The building blocks of social behavior, filmed with the earnest conviction that sandbox diplomacy prevents future wars.

items.title: Sharing Work At Home
items.description: Doing the dishes. Sweeping the floor. Setting the table. This film makes the case that household chores aren't punishment — they're your contribution to the family team.

items.title: Good Sportsmanship
items.description: Win with grace. Lose with dignity. Don't argue with the referee. The rules of sportsmanship applied to every aspect of life, not just the ball field.

items.title: Dropout, The (Part I)
items.description: Part One: A teenager drops out of high school. The reasons are complicated. The consequences are not. This two-part film follows the decision and its aftermath.

items.title: What About School Spirit?
items.description: School spirit isn't just about pep rallies and football games. It's about taking pride in your institution and contributing to something larger than yourself.

items.title: Unwelcome Affection
items.description: When someone's attention makes you uncomfortable, you have the right to say so. A guidance film about boundaries and unwanted contact that was ahead of its time.

items.title: It Takes All Kinds
items.description: Choose your marriage partner carefully, then accept what you chose. Personality analysis is the method, and the makers of Marriage for Moderns are behind it. Shop wisely: no returns.

items.title: Let's Share With Others
items.description: You have more than you need. Someone else has less. This film explains sharing not as sacrifice but as the foundation of community life.

items.title: Obligations
items.description: You made a promise. Now it's inconvenient to keep it. This film argues that obligations aren't optional — they're the glue that holds relationships and society together.

items.title: Understanding Others
items.description: Judge people on their true worth, not their money or manners, says a film in which a high school press club waits for a new editor and judges everyone in sight.

items.title: Other People's Property
items.description: Your neighbor's fence. The school's textbooks. The park bench. None of it is yours, and this film has strong feelings about how you should treat things that belong to other people.

items.title: The Other Fellow's Feelings
items.description: Before you say something hurtful, imagine how it would feel to hear it. This film teaches empathy through the simple act of considering the other person's perspective.

items.title: Learning to Live
items.description: A British social guidance film for teenagers, covering the facts of life with a stiff upper lip and educational charts. The accent is different but the awkwardness is universal.

items.title: Responsibility
items.description: Doing what you're supposed to do, even when no one is watching. This Herk Harvey film defines responsibility as the foundation of adult life and asks: are you ready?

items.title: Our Community
items.description: The fire department, the library, the school, the post office. How a community works, explained through the institutions that keep it running. Civic pride in 16mm.

items.title: The Good Loser
items.description: You lost the game. You didn't get the part. You came in second. This film teaches that losing well is more important than winning, because you'll do a lot more of it.

items.title: Dropout, The (Part II)
items.description: Part Two: The dropout discovers what life looks like without a diploma. The job market isn't kind. The future isn't bright. The film doesn't sugarcoat the consequences.

items.title: Turnabout Man
items.description: A man takes his road manners into the drawing room and his drawing room manners onto the road. Chevrolet paid for the lesson, which is to behave the same in both. Seat belts not included.

items.title: Are You Popular
items.description: What makes some teenagers popular and others not? This Coronet classic has theories — involving kindness, genuine interest in others, and not trying too hard.

items.title: Courtship and Marriage (Part II)
items.description: A Canadian engagement, complete with skating and a bridal shower, gets set beside a courtship in Kerala. Three hosts in a screening room explain both, with great confidence.

items.title: Date Etiquette
items.description: The etiquette of a 1952 date — from picking her up to bringing her home. Every gesture scrutinized, every social cue explained, every awkward moment anticipated and addressed.

items.title: When Should I Marry?
items.description: Are you old enough? Mature enough? Financially stable enough? This film has a checklist for marriage readiness that would disqualify most adults, let alone teenagers.

items.title: What Color Are You?
items.description: A 1967 examination of race, ethnicity, and skin color that asks children to think about what makes people different — and what makes them the same. Progressive for its era.

items.title: Discipline During Adolescence
items.description: A guide for parents struggling to understand their teenagers. The advice: listen more, lecture less, and remember that you were young once too. The parents in this film are trying their best.

items.title: Heritage
items.description: A 1940s animated film about the dangers of intolerance and totalitarianism. Heritage, freedom, and civic responsibility presented through the lens of American wartime values.

items.title: Appreciating Our Parents
items.description: Tommy is not a neat boy. His room is a mess, his clothes are dirty, and his mother is running out of patience. This film will fix Tommy. Or at least it will try.

items.title: 1949 Social Guidance Film "Exercise And Health"
items.description: A 1949 primer on physical fitness and healthy living. Exercise, fresh air, balanced meals, and eight hours of sleep — the prescription hasn't changed in seventy-five years.

items.title: "What Is Money?" - 1947 Educational Film
items.description: Where does money come from? What is it for? How does a bank work? A 1947 primer on basic economics that explains capitalism to children using coins and very small words.

items.title: The Responsibilities of American Citizenship
items.description: Responsible citizens learn to spot communist propaganda, says a film with strong views of its own to sell. Socialism, capitalism and public schools are on the syllabus too. Civics, Cold War edition.

items.title: The Town
items.description: A portrait of small-town America — its institutions, its people, and the way a community holds itself together. Civic pride filmed on location with genuine affection.

items.title: Practicing Democracy in the Classroom
items.description: Democracy isn't just something that happens in Washington. It happens in the classroom — every time students vote, debate, or learn to listen to someone they disagree with.

items.title: Citizen Makes a Decision, A
items.description: A citizen faces a local issue and must decide how to participate in the democratic process. Research, debate, voting — the machinery of self-governance, demonstrated at town hall scale.

items.title: Secure the Blessings
items.description: The blessings of liberty, secured by those who built this country and maintained by those who participate in its institutions. Civics education at its most sincere and patriotic.

items.title: Courtesy Comes to Town
items.description: A newspaper editor sends two teenagers out to find courtesy in the wild: a streetcar, a lunch counter, a shop, a taxi. They come back with a slogan. "Courtesy is the law and the profits." P-R-O-F-I-T-S. Somebody was very pleased with that.

items.title: Banks And Credits
items.description: How banks work, what credit means, and why saving money matters. Financial literacy for a generation that kept their money in passbooks and trusted the local savings and loan.

items.title: You and Your Friends
items.description: Your friends reflect who you are. Choose wisely. This film examines friendship as a moral exercise — you become like the people you spend time with.

items.title: Finding Your Life's Work
items.description: What do you want to be when you grow up? This guidance film helps you figure it out through aptitude tests, career research, and the revolutionary suggestion that you try things.

items.title: Driving Tips, Part 1
items.description: Mirrors, signals, and the art of not killing anyone. Driver's education presented with the calm authority of someone who has seen what happens when you don't check your blind spot.

items.title: Capitalism
items.description: A 1948 explanation of the capitalist system — free markets, private enterprise, and the profit motive. Taught to children as the natural order of economic life.

items.title: Don't Get Angry
items.description: You're furious. Your face is red. You want to break something. This film says: don't. Count to ten. Walk away. Come back when you can use your words like a civilized person.

items.title: The Dangerous Stranger
items.description: Don't take candy from strangers. Don't get in their car. Don't go anywhere with someone you don't know. A safety film that addresses every parent's worst fear with diagrams.

items.title: As the Twig Is Bent...
items.description: How early childhood shapes the adult you become. The twig is bent in its first years, and this film argues that good parenting and proper environment make all the difference.

items.title: How to Use Classroom Films
items.description: A training film for teachers on how to use films in the classroom. Meta-educational content — a film about watching films, projected on a projector for an audience of projector operators.

items.title: Film Research & Learning...
items.description: The science of using moving pictures to educate. Research methods, learning theory, and the earnest belief that a well-chosen filmstrip can change a child's life.

items.title: Darkness Before the Dawn: The "Pride of Judea" Story
items.description: A guidance film for troubled Jewish teenage boys, shot in New York and full of psychiatrists. With a title that grand, it is plainly not leaving the dawn to chance.

items.title: Wild at the Wheel
items.description: Reckless driving kills. This safety film has the statistics, the dramatic reenactments, and the narrator's disappointed tone to make sure you never forget it.

items.title: Live and Learn
items.description: Safety first — at home, at school, on the playground. A comprehensive guide to not hurting yourself, presented for children who seem determined to do exactly that.

items.title: The Dangerous Stranger (First Edition)
items.description: A police officer warns children about strangers, with the full Sid Davis dread of sidewalks and alleys. First of four editions, as if he thought one telling might not stick.

items.title: Out of This World
items.description: A literal angel and a literal devil monitor the daily performance of bread salesmen from the sky. Produced by DuPont to explain how cellophane packaging sells food. This was considered the clearest way to make that point.

items.title: Hired!
items.description: Jimmy the new salesman isn't hitting his numbers, and his sales manager wants to know why. A Chevrolet management film that slowly, carefully arrives at a radical conclusion: perhaps the problem is management.

items.title: Man to Man
items.description: Salesmanship and applied psychology for the firearms counter, 1947. Know your customer. Build rapport. Close the sale. The film assumes everyone involved is being completely reasonable, because it was that kind of era.

items.title: The Trouble With Women
items.description: A supervisor reports trouble with the women in his department, and the film reviews the complaint at length. The same irritated supervisor returns in The Grapevine. The file does not say whether he improved.

items.title: The Grapevine
items.description: Management would like office gossip studied. The film obliges, offending the overreacting manager, the nosy secretary and every participant in the grapevine. Nobody was consulted, and the word "girl" has aged badly.

items.title: Hidden Grievance
items.description: An employee keeps griping, but the real grievance is something else entirely — and now the union is involved. Part of a management training series that carefully presents the problem and then declines to solve it. You decide, foreman.

items.title: Promotion Bypass
items.description: The promotion goes to the younger man with the degree, and the film watches the older employee absorb it. Another in the Calvin management series, it supplies no answer. That was the exercise.

items.title: The Bright Young Newcomer
items.description: A promising young woman joins the office and the other women close ranks. The office manager elects to stand back and let it play out. A management training film about doing nothing, from the era when that was considered a technique.

items.title: The New Girl in the Office
items.description: The company has hired its first Black office worker, and the film studies the room. A quietly serious workplace-integration drama produced for management in 1960 — a year when this required a training film.

items.title: Office Etiquette
items.description: A complete do's-and-don'ts survey of office conduct: applying for the job, the first morning, routine duties, telephone courtesy. Success is presented as a series of small correct behaviors, performed daily, forever.

items.title: You Can Tell by the Teller
items.description: Training for the telephone company's business-office cashiers, with a heavy period dose of instruction on how the women at the counter should look and behave. The cash-handling procedures, at least, hold up.

items.title: The Things People Want
items.description: People don't buy products, this sales training film argues; they buy what products mean. A young John Forsythe, decades before Dynasty, lectures on the hierarchy of human needs. He sells the concept of wanting.

items.title: Trader Thorne
items.description: Why must a car dealership accept trade-ins? Because, the film explains with genuine resignation, nearly every customer already owns a car. An industry confronts market saturation and decides to film its feelings.

items.title: Selling America
items.description: A 1938 salesman receives sales advice from Benjamin Franklin. This is the generic version of a film originally produced for Frigidaire — meaning the ghost of Benjamin Franklin was retained and the refrigerator was cut.

items.title: Selling as a Career
items.description: One typical day with Art Williams, sporting-goods salesman: the reports filled out at home, the prospect estimates, the scheduled calls. Presented to young viewers as an aspiration. The paperwork is extensive.

items.title: The Selling Wizard
items.description: A film about moving more frozen food, starring the display freezer itself. At one point a pyramid of ice cream boxes collapses on camera. They left it in. The freezer's performance is otherwise flawless.

items.title: The Face in the Mirror (Part I)
items.description: Would you buy anything from the salesman you see in the mirror? Introspective psychology for sales staff, 1940: before you can close the customer, you must survive an honest look at yourself.

items.title: The Face in the Mirror (Part II)
items.description: The mirror examination continues. Having confronted himself in Part I, the salesman now rebuilds — attitude, approach, appearance — into someone he would buy from. The company finds this outcome acceptable.

items.title: International Moves the Browns to Sterling Street
items.description: A fictional family finds that installment buying puts silver tableware within reach, and International Silver's own salespeople are meant to take the lesson to heart. Selling silverware was a job, with meetings.

items.title: Two Pay Days (Part I)
items.description: A silent motivational film for 1927 Chevrolet salesmen. Two paydays, two salesmen, one lesson about effort. The intertitles do not blink and neither should you.

items.title: Two Pay Days (Part II)
items.description: The second reel. The diligent salesman and the coasting salesman arrive at very different paydays, exactly as management predicted. Management has always been predicting this.

items.title: The Troubles of a Merchant and How to Stop Them (Part II)
items.description: A storekeeper's business bleeds money until a National Cash Register is installed. Sponsored by NCR, whose president John H. Patterson more or less invented the corporate training film so he could make this exact point, repeatedly, on film.

items.title: Profile: Jamison Handy (Part I)
items.description: A 1961 television interview with Jam Handy — the man whose Detroit operation produced more corporate training films than anyone in history. The audio is low. Lean in. This is the person responsible for most of this channel.

items.title: Profile: Jamison Handy (Part II)
items.description: The interview continues. Handy built an empire on a single premise: that any problem an employee could have, a film could fix. Every tape on this channel is downstream of that belief.

items.title: Profile: Jamison Handy (Part III)
items.description: The conclusion of the Jam Handy interview. He produced films for decades, mostly for General Motors, at industrial scale. The industry he invented eventually stopped needing him, quietly, the way industries do.

items.title: The Open Door (Part I)
items.description: Foreman Jim Baxter learns to be a better manager, and also learns his place in the system of production. A General Motors film in which both lessons are presented as equally uplifting.

items.title: The Open Door (Part II)
items.description: Jim Baxter's education concludes. He is now a better foreman, a better family man, and a smoothly functioning component. General Motors is very proud of him.

items.title: Success in Business
items.description: A silent-era white-collar worker discovers the way to succeed in business. His reward is affluence and a happy family. The formula has been revised many times since without improving the ending.

items.title: The Inner Man Steps Out
items.description: A plant supervisor's job tension sends him to the doctor, who prescribes the principles of good supervision. An early sighting of the workplace-wellness genre: the diagnosis is management, and the cure is also management.

items.title: Ulcer at Work
items.description: Steve Hull is a white-collar man whose job pressure has produced an ulcer, and the ulcer is producing psychological extremes. Made when stress took the blame for ulcers; bacteria would not be named the cause until the 1980s.

items.title: Boredom at Work: The Empty Life
items.description: Hugh is bored at work, so he goes to a doctor about it. The doctor prescribes an all-consuming outside interest. The possibility that the work itself is the problem is never explored, by anyone, at any point.

items.title: Anger at Work: The Story of the Headache Switch
items.description: Workplace anger, explained by way of "the headache switch" — a mechanism somewhere inside you that your employer would prefer remain in the off position. A 1956 mental-hygiene film with a diagram's worth of confidence.

items.title: The Mullinaires
items.description: A chorus of kitchen salesmen sings an inspirational song to rally the rest of the sales force. This happened, was filmed, and was distributed as motivation. The song is about selling kitchens.

items.title: Another Cup of Coffee
items.description: Prudential teaches its insurance salesmen the five fundamentals of prospecting, largely over coffee. Everyone you have ever met is a prospect. Your neighbor is a prospect. Enjoy the coffee.

items.title: Helping You Sell
items.description: Excerpts from Direct Mass Selling films: auto salesmen, salesrooms, publicity stunts, a woman riding on the hood of a moving car. The 1930s believed absolutely anything could sell a car, and filmed all of it.

items.title: Studebaker Sales Training Film
items.description: A surviving fragment of a Studebaker sales training film: a test drive through oil-derrick California, a spirited price negotiation, a sales meeting. Studebaker no longer exists. The techniques remain in circulation.

items.title: Maintenance of Office Machines
items.description: The care and feeding of the typewriter, the dictaphone, the adding machine, and the calculator. Wartime office equipment was expected to last, and this film is a significant part of the reason it did.

items.title: How to Use the Dial Phone
items.description: The dial telephone has arrived, and the phone company is sincerely worried you cannot operate it. A complete 1927 training film on inserting your finger into a hole and rotating it. Take notes.

items.title: Operator Toll Dialing: Cord Signals
items.description: Bell System training for switchboard operators: what every lamp and cord signal means. A reminder that "operator, please" once dispatched a trained professional into a wall of cables on your behalf.

items.title: Operator Toll Dialing: Dialing
items.description: Part two of Bell's operator training regimen: the dialing itself. Precision, cadence, procedure. The company filmed the correct way to dial a telephone because there was, officially, a correct way.

items.title: Operator Toll Dialing: Teamwork
items.description: Bell operators learn that completing a long-distance call is a team effort. Corporate teamwork training from 1949, back when the team genuinely had to coordinate or the call did not happen.

items.title: Refreshment on the Job
items.description: Coca-Cola's case for on-the-job refreshment rests on three pillars: speak to workers in simple language, return your empties to the rack, and "mild stimulants go well with production." HR has reviewed this film and has questions.

items.title: How to Keep a Job
items.description: You got the job. This film is about not losing it: punctuality, attitude, appearance, initiative. Produced in 1949, and still the exact content of every onboarding module you have ever clicked through.

items.title: Office Courtesy: Meeting the Public
items.description: Front-desk training on how the office presents itself to visitors. Courtesy is framed as a company asset, which means your smile is, technically, inventory.

items.title: Telephone Courtesy
items.description: A full training film on answering the company telephone correctly. Identify yourself. Sound pleasant. Do not abandon the caller. Twenty-four minutes on this.

items.title: Duties of a Secretary
items.description: The duties of a secretary, cataloged in full: dictation, filing, telephone, appearance, discretion. A twenty-nine-minute job description from 1947, when the job description was also a lifestyle.

items.title: Help Wanted: Secretary
items.description: A harried executive lands on the psychiatrist's couch to recount his traumatic search for the perfect secretary, illustrated by three caricatures of poor office practice. The patient in therapy is the boss. This detail goes unexamined.

items.title: Cheechako: An Employee Orientation to Alaska
items.description: An orientation for employees transferring to Alaska — cheechakos, meaning newcomers. Covers the living and working conditions you can expect at your new posting. Your employer has relocated you past the edge of the map and prepared a film.

items.title: Welcome to San Jose: Employee Orientation
items.description: The Mayor and the City Manager personally welcome you, the new employee, to the City of San Jose. Department heads describe the new and exciting things they're involved with. It is January 1986. The enthusiasm is municipal.

items.id: mc-donalds-employee-training-video-doing-whatever-it-takes-1992/McDonald's Employee Training Video - Doing Whatever It Takes! (1992).ia.mp4
items.title: McDonald's: Doing Whatever It Takes!
items.description: The 1992 McDonald's crew tape on customer satisfaction. The title is also the policy: whatever it takes. Millions of teenagers received this exact pep talk in a back room, in uniform, on the clock.

items.title: Wendy's: New Employee Training
items.description: Your first day at Wendy's, 1987: the standards, the expectations, the Wendy's way of doing things — delivered with the total sincerity of a company that would shortly begin setting its training to music.

items.title: Wendy's: Hot Drinks
items.description: Wendy's teaches hot-drink preparation through the medium of rap. Two minutes and thirty-nine seconds of a man rhyming about coffee. This was real corporate training, and it worked — you will never forget it.

items.title: Wendy's: Cold Drinks
items.description: The companion piece: cold drinks, also sung. An employee learns to pour a soft drink from a man performing about it. The Wendy's training-video music program remains the high-water mark of the genre.

items.id: wendys-training-video-chili-can-be-served-with-cheese_202109/Wendys Training Video Chili Can Be Served With Cheese_480p.ia.mp4
items.title: Wendy's: Chili Can Be Served With Cheese
items.description: Wendy's clarifies, musically, that chili can be served with cheese. An entire production number exists to convey this single fact. The fact does stick.

items.title: Crystal Pepsi: Employee Training
items.description: Pepsi prepares its people to launch Crystal Pepsi, a clear cola positioned as the future of beverages. The training was thorough. The product was gone within two years. The tape outlived the product, which is how this channel works.

items.id: 1991-arco-ampm-employee-training-system-video-laserdisc/Classic Truly-Retro Training Videos/1962 Vincent Price Sales Training Video for Fine Art Collection.ia.mp4
items.title: ARCO am/pm: Employee Training System
items.description: ARCO's am/pm convenience stores trained employees by laserdisc in 1991 — a format considerably more advanced than most of the store. Interactive corporate training existed before the internet, and it looked like this.

items.id: rs-fo-107-conducting-the-new-employee-orientation/RS FO-107 Conducting the New Employee Orientation.mp4
items.title: Radio Shack: Conducting the New Employee Orientation
items.description: Radio Shack instructs its managers on how to conduct the new employee orientation — a training video about administering the training. Franchise Operations tape 107. The system had a system.

items.title: Tower Records: Handling Difficult Situations
items.description: Tower Records trains its clerks on handling difficult situations at the counter. The chain is gone now; the difficult situations continued without it.

items.title: AMC Theatres: Employee Training
items.description: AMC trains the class of 1997: the box office, the concession stand, the standards of the auditorium. Ten minutes that assume you will care deeply about someone else's movie theater. Remarkably, many did.

items.title: United Artists Theatres: General Employee Training
items.description: General employee training for United Artists Theatres, April 1993 — a movie chain teaching service standards on videotape while the features ran next door. The theaters are mostly gone. The training survived.

items.title: Hardee's Training Video
items.description: The 1987 Hardee's crew tape: counter service, standards, fundamentals — presented with the conviction of a chain that made you watch it in the break room on day one, before you had touched a register.

items.id: chuck-e-cheeses-university-training-1991-full-training/Chuck E  Cheese's University Training (1991) Full Training.mp4
items.title: Chuck E. Cheese's University Training
items.description: The complete Chuck E. Cheese's University curriculum, 1991 — nearly two hours of instruction for working at a pizza arcade. There is a university. You are enrolled. The animatronics are watching.

items.title: Pizza Hut Training Video
items.description: Pizza Hut trains the crew of 1988, back when Pizza Hut was a sit-down restaurant with a dining room. Seventeen minutes of a vanished restaurant format, preserved in training form.

items.title: Blockbuster: Buster Sales (Part 1)
items.description: Part one of Blockbuster's 1990 "Buster Sales" training. An eight-minute system for selling video rental, from a company that peaked at roughly nine thousand stores and currently operates one.

items.title: Blockbuster Employee Training
items.description: A 1990s Blockbuster training tape whose acting has become its legacy. The uploader titled it "Amazingly Bad." The uploader was being generous. The commitment of the cast, however, is total.

items.id: sunburstcommunicationssexualharassmentandhowtostopit1/Sunburst Communications - Sexual Harassment And How To Stop It_1.mp4
items.title: Sexual Harassment and How to Stop It
items.description: Sexual harassment and how to stop it, per a 1995 Sunburst Communications VHS. The scenarios are staged, the wardrobe is authentic, and the subject matter, unfortunately, never went out of date.

items.title: Sexual Harassment: Stop It Now
items.description: A 1997 workplace tape whose title is also the entire training: stop it now. Direct, procedural, and mandatory in the fullest sense of this channel's name.

items.id: TheVistaGroup-SexualHarassmentTechniquesforElimination1997/1997 VHS Sexual Harassment, Techniques for Elimination 60 FPS.ia.mp4
items.title: Sexual Harassment: Techniques for Elimination
items.description: Techniques for Elimination: nearly ninety minutes of 1997 harassment training. The title sounds like an action film. The content is very much not. This is some of the most nineteen-ninety-seven workplace footage in existence.

items.title: Sexual Harassment: A Common Sense Approach
items.description: Workplace harassment training, the common-sense edition — a VHS that believes the problem can be solved by everyone simply being reasonable. This explains both the title and the continued existence of every other tape on the subject.

items.title: Apple II Training
items.description: Apple trains the office on the Apple II. In 1980, a computer arrived at your desk accompanied by a tape, and the tape assumed — correctly — that you had never touched a computer.

items.title: System 7 Presentations Training
items.description: Apple's official video on giving presentations with System 7. Twenty-six minutes of 1991 desktop confidence, from the era when "multimedia" was a word you said in meetings to get budget.

items.title: Commodore 64 Training Tape
items.description: Jim Butterfield — the most patient man in home computing — walks you through the Commodore 64 for nearly two hours. Sold as a training tape; functionally a benediction. Bring a notepad.

items.title: VAX 9000 Sales Video
items.description: Digital Equipment's sales video for the VAX 9000 — the fastest, most expensive VAX ever built, pitched against IBM's mainframes with total confidence. DEC was gone within the decade. The confidence is preserved here.

items.id: thevistagroup-aolamericaonlineinccorporatevideo1990s_/AOL America Online Inc Corporate Video VHS • 60 FPS 1990s.ia.mp4
items.title: AOL Corporate Video
items.description: America Online explains itself in five minutes of corporate overview, produced when "online" still required a definition. Aimed at prospective partners and subscribers. Eventually, everyone got the free trial anyway.

items.title: Attitude Is Everything
items.description: Sales trainer Tom Hopkins delivers Attitude Is Everything, 1996: sixteen minutes of pure motivational payload for the salesperson whose numbers are down and whose manager owns this tape.

items.title: Stay Safe, Stay Strong: The Facts About Nuclear Weapons
items.description: Comfort first, facts second: the whole civil defense method, aimed at nuclear weapons. It opens with aerials of Washington before the mushroom cloud, so the order of events is at least honest.

items.title: Science in Action: Radar Defense Screen
items.description: A kinescope of Science in Action. Host Earl Herald has an Air Force brigadier general at the plotting table to explain radar defense. The last two minutes are Animal of the Week, a parrot. Same calm for both.

items.title: Duck and Cover (Prelinger Print)
items.description: Bert the Turtle had one piece of advice for surviving nuclear annihilation: duck under your desk and cover your neck. Reassuringly, the government considered this a complete plan.

items.id: 52934CivilDefenseFireFightingForHouseholders/52934 Civil Defense Fire Fighting For Householders.mp4
items.title: Fire Fighting for Householders
items.description: The Federal Civil Defense Administration explains how to put out your own house fires once an atomic bomb has gone off. The theme is to be prepared, delivered with a fire bell and total composure.

items.title: In Our Hands: How to Lose What We Have
items.description: Part three of four. A coup comes to an American town helped along by apathy, and the film treats a lapsed civic duty as seriously as the siren. Bring a ballot, not a shelter.

items.title: Science in Action: Radar Defense Screen
items.description: A brigadier general explains how radar will protect America from airborne nuclear attack. The host nods along like this is a cooking segment. Kinescope from a 1950s science TV show.

items.title: The H-Bomb
items.description: The Home Office shows Britain's rescue crews what a ten-megaton bomb would do to a city, with scale models, animation and wartime footage. The narration is somber throughout. No jokes, which is correct.

items.title: Atomic Weapons Tests: Trinity through Buster-Jangle
items.description: Once a secret briefing for congressional oversight committees, now cleared for everyone, with the sensitive parts taken out first. The early run of American atomic tests, in order.

items.title: The House in the Middle
items.description: The paint industry and the federal government agree: a clean, freshly painted house has the survival edge in a nuclear blast. Housekeeping as defense policy. The National Film Registry kept a copy.

items.title: Our Cities Must Fight
items.description: The government would like you to stay in your city during a nuclear attack. Not to survive, necessarily, but to fight. For the city. This film explains why fleeing is unpatriotic.

items.title: Survival Under Atomic Attack (Prelinger Print)
items.description: Edward R. Murrow narrates your chances of surviving an atomic bomb with the calm authority of a man explaining a weather forecast. The forecast is not good, but the tone is lovely.

items.title: Operation Cue
items.description: Furnished houses in the Nevada desert, mannequins dressed and seated, and one very large flash. Civil defense wanted you to see what happens to a living room. The advice is to be elsewhere.

items.title: About Fallout (1963)
items.description: The later of the two About Fallout films here: what fallout is, how it settles, what to do about it. The tone is so even you start to believe it, which may be the point. Take notes.

items.title: Milford, U.S.A.
items.description: Milford rehearses the worst day in a Red Cross shelter and a fallout shelter, then talks it over. A simulated disaster is the gentlest kind, which is why the town practices it.

items.title: Operation Plumbbob: Military Effects Studies
items.description: The Air Force's Lookout Mountain Laboratory films the Nevada tests as a binder of reports: shelters, underground readings, instruments. No fireball. Just the measurements that decided how shelters get built.

items.title: Fallout: When and How to Protect Yourself
items.description: An animated primer on fallout: what it is, what it does, and how to protect your food and water. Devo used it in the Beautiful World video, so the tone has been vouched for.

items.title: What to Do in a Gas Attack
items.description: How to get through a chemical attack with what you already own, in the cheerful voice of a wartime public service film. It wants you ready. The tone says you already are.

items.title: Nursing Care of the Sick and Injured
items.description: Part of the Medical Self-Help series, for a shelter where no doctor is coming. Temperatures, an isolation room, close-ups of rashes. It ends on a hall of cots, and you are the staff.

items.title: Food Supply After the Bomb
items.description: After the bomb, the farms are gone and the water is suspect, so the plan is a ten-day Emergency Food Box of canned goods. The narrator is very confident about the box.

items.title: Radiological Defense
items.description: Written like a pamphlet: sit down, here is how to think about fallout, and here is the arithmetic. The tone says tidy basement. The subject says otherwise, and the tone never notices.

items.title: In Our Hands: How We Got What We Have
items.description: A young couple and their baby start in the wilderness with nothing but their hands, to show why tools matter. Part one of four, so the case for private ownership has time to settle in.

items.title: Your Chance to Live: Earthwatch
items.description: A teenage couple and a tsunami. The government's contribution to disaster dating advice, wrapped in a primer on earthquakes. Part of the optimistically titled 'Your Chance to Live' series.

items.title: Battle of the United States
items.description: J. Edgar Hoover warns the nation about enemy spies — with footage from American Nazi rallies at Madison Square Garden to prove his point. The threat is inside the house. Literally.

items.title: Rescue Reconnaissance
items.description: A dramatized training film on how to dig people out of bombed buildings. Step one: assess the wreckage. Step two: listen for signs of life. Step three: try not to think about why you need this skill.

items.title: News Magazine of the Screen: Atomic Energy
items.description: A newsreel compilation of 1950s atomic highlights: weapons testing, civil defense drills, and the promise of nuclear energy. All the optimism of the Atomic Age in one convenient reel.

items.title: Facts Make the Difference
items.description: An Office of Civil Defense training film on the dull middle of a warning: who, what, when, where, why. Someone has to write it down before the sirens mean anything. The film assigns that job to men at desks.

items.title: One Week in October
items.description: The Cuban Missile Crisis as Civil Defense showed it to theaters: aerial photos of missile sites, a blockade, the UN. The office that made it asked if civil defense had no glamor. It tried, calmly.

items.title: Pattern for Survival
items.description: A museum guide walks a young visitor past old weapons to explain that people keep building what they struggle to understand. Then the mushroom cloud. One of the earliest civil defense films.

items.title: Atomic Alert
items.description: A film teaching children the basic methods of protecting themselves from an atomic bomb explosion. The methods are: get under something. That's it. That's the method.

items.title: The Invisible Enemy
items.description: A professor explains radiation, which you cannot see and cannot argue with. Partway in, the film simulates an attack on Chicago and follows the fallout cloud outward, patiently, like a weather map.

items.title: The Big Picture: The Steel Ring
items.description: The Army's Big Picture tours the radars and guns ringed around American cities. There will be no warning, so be ready. Reassuring, in the sense that someone is standing watch.

items.title: About Fallout (1955)
items.description: The earlier of the two About Fallout films here, Jack Tilles directing. Its message is that the worry is bigger than the problem, and it says so with total confidence. Go back to your yard work.

items.title: To Live Tomorrow
items.description: An insurance agent on a train looks at his fellow passengers and wonders how they'd handle an atomic attack. The life insurers made it, with an Eisenhower introduction. Nobody on board panics yet.

items.title: Communism
items.description: A classroom film on the Cold War's main opponent, in the calm voice of a school that has already decided the answer. Short, orderly, very sure of itself. Please keep your desk clear.

items.title: You Can Change the World
items.description: The Christophers, a Catholic group whose motto was to light one candle rather than curse the darkness, put Crosby, Hope and Benny in a living room. A priest talks. The stars are there to sit and nod.

items.title: Life-Line of the Nation
items.description: American railroads: keeping the nation's supply lines moving during wartime. Troops, food, ammunition — all delivered on time by the backbone of democracy. A love letter to logistics.

items.title: Shelter on a Quiet Street
items.description: Civil Defense Director Hank Adams guides the Warren family through a concrete basement shelter, and the pitch is that it is easy and economical. Home improvement with one very specific purpose.

items.title: What You Should Know About Biological Warfare
items.description: Three types of biological warfare: germs, toxins, and plant growth regulators. This film explains all three and what you, a regular citizen, should do about them. The answer is mostly vigilance.

items.title: Communist Blueprint for Conquest
items.description: Boris Klosson of the State Department explains how a party seizes a country, in an Armed Forces Information Film. Our copy begins mid-lesson, which is how most of us took in civics.

items.title: The Sky Is Your Target
items.description: Ordinary volunteers watch the sky for enemy bombers, and the Air Force would like you to know it's a real job. Calm, patient work, pointed at the one thing you hope never shows up.

items.title: Security Is Your Responsibility
items.description: Lock your file cabinets. Shred your documents. Trust no one in the break room. A Cold War workplace security film that makes every office feel like a spy thriller.

items.title: Communism: Riddle, Mystery, Enigma
items.description: The Soviet Army, briefed calmly: its size, its oath, its daily schedule, and its pay next to the U.S. Army's. Everything is explained in a steady voice. That is how you know it matters.

items.title: The Decision to Drop the Bomb
items.description: NBC's documentary on the Hiroshima decision, cut down for classrooms by Britannica. Mostly older men in chairs, speaking in order. The ruins arrive at the end, and the film lets them.

items.title: Red Nightmare
items.description: Jerry Donovan shrugs off his civic duties, then wakes up in a town run by Communists. Jack Webb hosts, with his usual Dragnet calm. The lesson is to go to the meetings, which seems like a fair ask.

items.title: Atomic Alert (Elementary Version)
items.description: The elementary school version of nuclear preparedness. Smaller words, same existential dread. Aimed at children who can't yet spell 'thermonuclear' but need to survive one.

items.title: Face of Disaster
items.description: The bomb is not in this one. Earthquake, flood, tornado, hurricane, and then the welfare workers and ham radio operators who show up. Civil defense was always meant to cover more than the one disaster.

items.title: Medical Aspects of Nuclear Radiation
items.description: Animation good enough that you nearly forget to check the thesis, which is that radiation is not so dangerous. Check the thesis. It is a well-made, calm film, and a hard one to take at its word.

items.title: A Day Called X (Part I)
items.description: Part one of the dramatized evacuation of Portland, Oregon under atomic threat. The whole city participates. Everyone is calm, organized, and following the plan. It's very convincing if you don't think about it.

items.title: Civil Defence Bulletins
items.description: Made in the early 1960s to air as nuclear war approached, and never aired, which is the best review a bulletin can get. The Civil Defence Corps saw them in training. The uploader confirms there is no part 8.

items.title: A Day Called X (Part II)
items.description: Part two. Portland is still evacuating. The sirens are still going. The plan is still working perfectly, which is the most fictional part of this dramatization.

items.title: The Homeless Ones
items.description: A Canadian cartoon about an atomic attack on a city, made for civil defense welfare workers, and terribly grim. The pamphlet voice says organize, train and prepare. The animation says why.

items.title: Plowshare
items.description: What if we used nuclear bombs for construction? Mining? Civil engineering? The Atomic Energy Commission's 'Plowshare' program makes the case for peaceful detonations. What could go wrong?

items.title: Taking the X out of X-Rays
